pages.text: Earthquakes

image.note: Cover: the ground cracking, a city skyline beyond

pages.text: Contents. When the Ground Shakes / The Restless Earth / Why Earthquakes Happen / Measuring the Shaking / Staying Safe / The Earth Never Rests.

The ground beneath your feet feels perfectly still, solid, and safe. It seems the one thing in all the world you can truly rely on. And yet, right now, it is moving. Slowly, quietly, the very ground is shifting, and every so often, somewhere on earth, it shifts all at once, and shakes. This is the story of earthquakes, and the restless world we stand upon.

image.note: A child standing on ground that hides deep cracks

pages.text: For most of history, people did not know why the ground shook. They told stories of giants turning in their sleep, or great beasts stirring under the earth. The truth, worked out only recently, is stranger still: the solid ground is not solid at all, but a set of vast slabs, floating, and forever slowly on the move.

image.note: An old myth of a beast beneath the earth beside the real explanation

pages.text: An earthquake is exactly what it sounds like: a shaking of the earth. Sometimes it is so gentle that only instruments can feel it. Sometimes it is strong enough to rattle windows, or to rock a whole city. The ground rolls and trembles, often for less than a minute, and then, as suddenly as it came, it is still again.

image.note: The ground trembling, objects shaking

pages.text: Where do they happen? Not evenly across the world. If you mark every earthquake on a map, they line up in long, clear lines across the earth, as if tracing a hidden pattern. Those lines are the great secret of earthquakes, and to understand them, we must look far beneath our feet.

image.note: A world map with earthquakes tracing clear lines

pages.text: Deep below the ground you stand on, the earth is not solid all the way down. Beneath the thin, hard crust we live on lies rock so hot it can slowly move, like extremely thick, creeping treacle. And floating upon it, like the cracked shell of a boiled egg, the hard outer crust is broken into enormous pieces called plates.

image.note: A cutaway of the earth: crust, hot rock, moving plates

pages.text: These plates are gigantic, whole countries and oceans ride upon them. And they are moving, all the time, carried along on the slow-flowing hot rock beneath, about as fast as your fingernails grow. Far too slowly to feel. But over millions of years, they carry the continents right across the world.

image.note: Vast plates carrying continents, moving slowly

pages.text: The plates are always on the move, and where two of them meet, there is trouble. Sometimes they grind slowly past each other. Sometimes one pushes against another. And as they press and push, they do not slide smoothly. They catch, and stick, and the pressure builds, and builds, for years.

image.note: Two great plates pressing and catching at their edge

pages.text: Then, at last, the stuck rock can bear the strain no longer, and it suddenly slips, all at once, releasing all that stored-up pressure in an instant. That sudden slip sends waves shuddering out through the ground in every direction, and those waves, reaching the surface, are the shaking we feel. That is an earthquake.

image.note: Stuck rock suddenly slipping, waves spreading out

pages.text: This is why earthquakes trace those lines across the map. The lines are the edges of the great plates, where they meet and grind. Some places sit right on these edges and feel many earthquakes; others sit safely in the middle of a plate and feel almost none. It is all down to what lies far below.

image.note: Earthquake lines matching the edges of the plates

pages.text: When the ground shakes, scientists want to know exactly how strongly. So they use a clever instrument called a seismograph, so sensitive it can feel a tremble far too faint for any person, and draw it as a jagged line, recording the earth's every shiver.

image.note: A seismograph drawing a jagged line of shaking

pages.text: From these records, scientists give each earthquake a number, to say how strong it was. A small number means a gentle tremble that does little harm. A large number means a powerful quake. Each step up the scale means far more shaking than the step below, so a large quake is many times stronger than a small one.

image.note: A scale of earthquake strength, small to large

pages.text: Scientists who study earthquakes are called seismologists, and they watch the earth day and night, all over the world. They cannot yet say exactly when an earthquake will strike. But they know where they are most likely, and they work hard to help people in those places prepare, and stay safe.

image.note: Seismologists monitoring the earth

pages.text: In places where earthquakes are common, people have learned to live with them wisely. They build their houses and towers specially, to sway and bend a little without breaking, so that even a strong quake need not bring them down. Clever building has saved countless lives.

image.note: An earthquake-safe building designed to sway

pages.text: Children in these places practise what to do, so they are never caught by surprise. When the ground shakes, the advice is simple: drop down low, take cover under something strong like a sturdy table, and hold on until the shaking stops. Being ready, and staying calm, makes all the difference.

image.note: Children calmly taking cover under a sturdy table

pages.text: Earthquakes can be dangerous, it is true, and the strongest have caused great harm. But knowledge is a powerful shield. The more we understand why the ground shakes, and the better we build and prepare, the more we can keep people safe when the restless earth stirs.

image.note: A prepared, well-built town at peace

pages.text: So the solid ground is not so solid after all. It is the thin, cracked shell of a restless world, its great plates forever drifting, grinding, and, now and then, slipping with a shudder we feel as an earthquake. The very same slow movements, over ages, raise mountains and shape the continents themselves.

image.note: The living, moving earth shaping mountains and lands

pages.text: It is a strange and humbling thought, that the ground beneath you, which seems so still, is quietly, endlessly on the move, and always will be. The earth is not finished. It is alive with slow, tremendous power, and every earthquake is a small reminder of the vast and restless world we call home.

image.note: A child standing thoughtfully on the living earth

pages.text: Words to know. Crust: the thin, hard outer layer of the earth we live on. Plate: one of the great slabs the crust is broken into. Seismograph: the instrument that measures shaking. Seismologist: a scientist who studies earthquakes. Fault: a line where two plates meet and grind.

image.note: Labelled diagram of the earth's plates and a fault

pages.text: The same restless power that shakes the ground also builds mountains, opens oceans, and, sometimes, bursts out as a volcano. The earth beneath you has many more stories to tell. Which will you dig into next?

image.note: The powerful, living earth: mountains, oceans, a volcano
